task: This is a synthetic newspaper-writing exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes. Write from the reporting snapshot as of September 8, 2026. Write a headline and a 450–650-word AP-style reported feature about how the bus timetable shapes working days at Rillstone Switchgear and the practical choices behind a proposed employer shuttle.

facts.text: A field note from Aug. 6, 2026, follows assembler Omi Doren from the 6:05 a.m. bus arrival to Rillstone Switchgear, a seven-minute walk away.
Doren's shift begins at 6:15 a.m., leaving three minutes between the normal walk's end and the scheduled start.
The shift ends at 2:15 p.m., and the return bus leaves at 2:25 p.m. from the same stop.
Missing that departure usually means waiting an hour for the next bus under the current weekday timetable.
Doren does not own a car and sometimes declines optional extra work at the end of the shift because of the return connection.
Doren said, "Ten more minutes at the bench can become an hour at the bus stop."
The factory has 85 employees, and 40 answered its voluntary commuting survey.
Fourteen respondents said they regularly depended on the bus; the survey does not establish the commuting choices of nonrespondents.
The factory's production line includes a shared morning briefing, making completely different start times difficult for some jobs.
Production manager Teri Vann has requested a quote for a shuttle between the central bus interchange and the factory.
A local operator quoted $140 per working day for a limited morning-and-afternoon pilot, or $2,800 for 20 working days.
The employer has not approved the pilot budget or selected a start date.
The public bus operator says its vehicles also serve school journeys and cannot simply move this route's departures without affecting other runs.
Driver Leda Quill said the published timetable is a chain of trips rather than a separate vehicle waiting for each factory shift.
Quill said, "Moving one departure means deciding which other passengers will wait."
The proposed shuttle would serve a single employer, not replace the town's public bus route.
The factory has six advertised vacancies, but its recruitment records do not isolate transport as the cause of those vacancies.
Doren says a reliable connection would matter more to her than a workplace parking benefit.
The factory makes electrical cabinets on an industrial estate developed before the current housing expansion.
The reporting record contains no adopted bus-route cut, attendance penalty against Doren or confirmed hiring increase from a shuttle.

forbidden_additions: An approved shuttle, public-route closure or proven transport cause for all vacancies
Fourteen bus-dependent respondents represent every worker or Doren was disciplined
